questions.enonce_markdown:
Define the following terms:

(i) Excretion.

(ii) Osmoregulation. *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Excretion** is the **removal from the body of the waste products of metabolism** (for example **urea, ammonia, uric acid, carbon dioxide, bile pigments**) and of **excess substances**, which would be toxic if they accumulated.

**(ii) Osmoregulation** is the **control of the water and salt (solute) content of the body fluids**, that is, of their **osmotic pressure (water potential)**, so that it is **kept constant within narrow limits**. In mammals it is done mainly by the **kidneys**, under the control of the **hypothalamus and antidiuretic hormone (ADH)**.

(2 marks for each definition.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Describe how ultrafiltration takes place in the nephron of the kidney. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Where.** Ultrafiltration takes place in the **Malpighian body (renal corpuscle)**, between the **glomerulus** (a knot of capillaries) and the **Bowman's capsule** (the cup-shaped end of the nephron).

**How the high pressure is built up**
1. Blood comes from the renal artery through the **afferent arteriole**, which is **wider** than the **efferent arteriole** that carries blood away from the glomerulus.
2. This difference of diameter creates a **resistance to the outflow**, so the blood in the glomerular capillaries is under **high hydrostatic pressure**.
3. This pressure is **greater than the opposing forces**: the **hydrostatic pressure of the fluid in the capsule** and the **osmotic (oncotic) pressure of the plasma proteins** (low water potential of the blood). The **net filtration pressure is therefore positive** and pushes fluid out of the capillaries.

**The filtration barrier (three layers between blood and capsule space)**
1. The **endothelium of the glomerular capillary**, whose cells have **tiny pores (fenestrations)**; blood cells cannot pass.
2. The **basement membrane**, a gel of glycoproteins and collagen fibres acting as the **main molecular filter**: it holds back **large molecules** (relative molecular mass above about 68 000, such as plasma proteins).
3. The **podocytes**, cells of the inner wall of the capsule, whose foot-like processes leave **filtration slits** through which the filtrate passes.

**The filtrate.** **Water, glucose, amino acids, urea, mineral ions (Na+, K+, Cl-), vitamins and other small molecules** pass into the capsule space, forming the **glomerular filtrate** (about 125 cm³ per minute, 180 dm³ per day in humans). **Blood cells and plasma proteins stay in the blood**. The filtrate then flows into the proximal convoluted tubule.

*Diagram expected:* a labelled drawing of the Malpighian body showing the afferent and efferent arterioles, the glomerulus, the three layers and the capsule space.

(Marking: pressure difference, the three layers, what passes and what does not.)

questions.enonce_markdown: How is concentrated urine produced in humans? *[6 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Concentrated urine is produced when the body is **short of water** (little drinking, sweating, diarrhoea), by the **loop of Henle, the collecting duct and ADH**.

1. **The loop of Henle builds up a high solute concentration in the medulla (counter-current multiplier).** The **ascending limb is impermeable to water** and its walls **pump Na+ and Cl- out by active transport** into the tissue fluid of the medulla. The **descending limb is permeable to water** and **water leaves it by osmosis**, so the filtrate becomes more concentrated towards the tip of the loop. The result is a gradient: the **medulla tissue fluid has a very low water potential (high solute concentration), increasing from the cortex to the inner medulla**. The **vasa recta** (blood vessels running parallel) keep the gradient by counter-current exchange.
2. When the **water potential of the blood falls**, **osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus** detect it and the **posterior lobe of the pituitary gland releases more antidiuretic hormone (ADH)**.
3. **ADH makes the walls of the distal convoluted tubule and collecting duct more permeable to water** (more **aquaporins** are inserted in the membranes).
4. As the filtrate passes down the **collecting duct through the medulla**, which has a low water potential, **a large amount of water leaves the duct by osmosis** and is taken away by the blood capillaries.
5. A **small volume of concentrated (hypertonic) urine** is produced. When the body has too much water the process is reversed: less ADH, walls less permeable, large volume of dilute urine. The system works by **negative feedback**.

(Marking: loop of Henle and the medulla gradient, ADH and permeability, water reabsorption in the collecting duct.)

questions.enonce_markdown: Why do plants not send out nitrogenous waste? *[2 marks]* *(4, 8, 6, 2 marks)*
questions.corrige_markdown:
1. Plants **do not eat protein in excess** and make **only the amino acids and proteins they need**, so they **do not break down surplus amino acids (no deamination)** and produce very little nitrogenous waste, compared with animals.
2. Any nitrogenous by-products (for example ammonia) are **reused to make new amino acids, proteins and nucleic acids**, and the small remaining amount can be **stored harmlessly in vacuoles** or **lost in old leaves, bark and fruits when they fall**.

(One mark for each point.)
